rules.statement: Keep an `.Abstractions` package to contracts and data only: put no logic (helpers with behavior, default implementations) in it.
rules.why: Abstractions hold no logic so that a consumer can take the contracts without an implementation; a helper with logic belongs in an implementation or foundation package.
rules.check: Look for new types in an `*.Abstractions` project that contain method bodies with real logic, extension helpers that compute something, or default service implementations.

rules.statement: Give a capability's implementation package the same namespace as its `.Abstractions` package, so the pair is one namespace across two assemblies.
rules.why: A pair is meant to be one namespace across two assemblies, so consumers find contracts and implementation together.
rules.check: Compare the root namespace of new types in an implementation project with the namespace of the contracts they implement in the matching `.Abstractions` project.

rules.statement: Don't let an implementation project reference another implementation project; collaborate through the other capability's abstractions resolved from DI, leaving only composition roots, hosts and a documented layered framework reference (such as an Entity Framework slice referencing the EF framework it plugs into) as exceptions.
rules.why: Implementation-to-implementation references bring transitive dependencies, make the package boundary meaningless and lose independent replaceability.
rules.check: Inspect `.csproj` `ProjectReference`/`PackageReference` changes in implementation projects for references to non-`.Abstractions`, non-foundation implementation projects that are not composition roots or hosts.

rules.statement: Register a package's default services with `TryAdd*` so a consumer can replace them.
rules.why: Consumers implement, decorate or replace a capability; `TryAdd*` lets a prior registration win.
rules.check: Look for `services.AddSingleton/AddScoped/AddTransient` calls in a library's registration extension where `TryAdd*` should be used.

rules.statement: Don't name a package for who uses it (`.Common`, `.Shared`, `.Utilities`, `.Helpers`); name it for the capability it provides.
rules.why: A package named for its users mixes capabilities and cannot be taken or replaced as one capability.
rules.check: Check new project, package or assembly names for suffixes like `.Common`, `.Shared`, `.Utilities`, `.Helpers`.

rules.statement: Share code between packages through a public package, never through linked source files.
rules.why: Linked shared source makes every consumer compile its own copy, and the copies drift.
rules.check: Look for `<Compile Include="..\..." Link=...>` items in `.csproj` files that pull source from another project.

rules.statement: Keep a type public once it is public, and place it in the package whose capability it is, rather than moving it to internal or into an unrelated package.
rules.why: Package IDs and public surface are permanent once published; a type belongs with its capability so consumers take one pair to get it.
rules.check: Look for public types made internal or moved into a package of a different capability.

rules.statement: Don't add a `Microsoft.AspNetCore.App` `FrameworkReference` to a contract package unless its contracts are HTTP types.
rules.why: Contracts that carry a heavy framework dependency force every consumer of the contract to take that framework too.
rules.check: Inspect `.Abstractions` `.csproj` changes for a new `FrameworkReference Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.App"` where the public contracts expose no ASP.NET Core/HTTP types.

rules.statement: Create a new shared foundation package only when a second package consumes it, and let it reference only other foundation packages; a capability only one package uses stays in that package.
rules.why: A foundation package that only one package consumes is a sign the split was wrong.
rules.check: For a new shared/foundation project, verify at least two packages reference it and it references no capability implementation.

rules.statement: Truncate times that round-trip through a JWT `NumericDate` to whole seconds using the shared whole-second helpers, not with inline truncation at each call site.
rules.why: Inlined copies drift, and then a stored time differs from the `NumericDate` it round-trips through a JWT.
rules.check: Look for ad-hoc truncation such as `AddTicks(-(x.Ticks % TimeSpan.TicksPerSecond))` or `FromUnixTimeSeconds(ToUnixTimeSeconds())` on token times instead of the shared `WithPrecisionInSeconds()`/`GetUtcNowWithPrecisionInSeconds()` helpers.
